Conceded: risk-management as a formal discipline predates error-prevention. Risk management emerged from actuarial science (1930s) and became systematic in the mid-20th century. Error-prevention evolved as a focused offshoot within that broader framework, zeroing in on human and organizational error as a specific risk category. The which-came-first test passes: risk-management existed first and fed into the more specialized error-prevention discipline.

Safety-management as a framework contains individual safety programs as structural parts. The note passes the removal test: removing all programs from the management system leaves it without operational content — it becomes an empty shell. This is a genuine whole-part relationship at the institutional level, not a kind-of relationship. A management system's structure is constituted by the programs it contains.

On reconsideration: the scope clearly describes a human-made construct — a sign, metric, or signal deliberately designed to convey information about the state of a system. It is on the made side (Law 1), with a clear persistence mechanism in language and standardized practice. The carving is sufficient: not all signs are indicators, only those deliberately designed for conveying system-state information.

CONTAINS (Law 10) requires whole-and-part. Safety objectives are goals/outcomes the program aims to achieve — they are not constituent physical or structural parts. A goal is a direction, not a piece. This edge mislabels teleology as composition.

CONTAINS Law 10 fails: objectives are goals/outcomes a program aims at, not constituent parts. A program is not a container with objectives as physical or structural parts. This is DEPENDS_ON at best, not a whole-and-part.
